reason: Question, answer, and future-honor sentences all match their cases and persons; h₂éyeri is the real 'in the morning' locative.
English 'will he come here' uses a verb the engine glosses as 'swell', not 'come'.
All roles and cases fit; neuter plural subjects take singular verbs as in archaic PIE collectives.
'Carry the water' needs accusative singular wódr̥; wédnōm is genitive plural.
Imperatives, subjunctives, and predicates agree with their subjects and match the English.
Question 'Did he devour the goat?' needs 3SG past (gʷr̥h₃ét), but gʷr̥h₃éte is 2PL.
English 'Did you fight over the spring?' uses 'vow' (h₁wogʷʰéyeti), not 'fight' (wikéti as in the next line).
'Another village' is singular, but h₂élyoyh₁ is a neuter dual and does not agree with ḱóymōd.
English 'no wolf came' is negated, but the PIE clause has no ne.
Direct address 'sister-in-law' needs the vocative (ǵl̥h₂ow, as in J12), not the locative ǵl̥h₂éwi.
Definitions, comparatives, ablatives, and imperatives all match the English.
The object is 'the pot' (kʷérom), but bʰléh₁wom is the adjective 'colorful'.
'The old man' is masculine, but ǵr̥h₂n̥tyéh₂i is feminine locative singular.
Dual noun with dwóh₁ 'two' is the same pattern used elsewhere for paired counts; other forms agree.
Vow, protect, and imperative forms match their subjects and objects.
Past, future, and imperative forms match; the negated prohibition and denial are present.
The vocative addresses 'Grandmother' but stéla is the vocative of 'earth mound'.
English 'the immortals will protect him' needs 'protect' (h₂lékseti in J20), but the engine glosses déwh₂onti as 'join together'.
English 'Do they not eat the wheat?' is negated, but the PIE question has no ne.
Dual twin clause, genitives, ablatives, and final future all agree.
English 'I grasp it' is present, but h₁épm̥ is aorist (past) 1SG.
'By the fire' needs the word for fire (h₁n̥gʷnís locative), but h₃n̥gʷéni means 'fat'.
Genitives, accusatives, and subjunctive/past forms match the English.
'It does not love her' is negated, but the PIE clause has no ne.
Cases, tenses, and the augmentless injunctive forms match the English.
Genitive and accusative objects and the optative blessing agree with the English.
The imperatives and 'you' address one villager, but logʰéyete and téth₂gete are 2PL; h₂éd is also not a usable form here.
Negated clauses and case-marked objects match; h₂ew reads as 'again' in the same way as the other items.
'On the earth' needs dʰéǵʰōm, but donḱéh₂i is locative of 'tongs'.
'Wealth' is singular in the English, but h₃épnesih₁ is dual.
English 'the wind does not shake it' is negated, but the PIE clause has no ne.
'Dearer to him' needs a comparative of 'dear', but kéh₂yōs is glossed as 'heat'.
Numerals, cases, and the conditional clause match the English.
'Your wife was not giving me food' is negated, but the PIE clause has no ne.
Genitives, ablatives, locatives, and subjunctive forms agree with the English.
Dual and singular subjects, cases, and imperatives match their roles.
Vocatives, genitives, datives, and imperatives match their roles.
English 'You owe me nothing' is negative, but the PIE clause has kʷid with no ne.
'From my field' needs the ablative (h₂égrōd) after swṓd, but h₂éǵros is nominative.
Augmentless past with mē gives the prohibition, and the other forms match the English.
'My wife will not sleep here' is negated, but the PIE clause has no ne.
Locatives, accusatives, and the optative blessing all match the English.
Ablatives, datives, and subjunctive forms match the English.
The subject 'a goose came forth' is replaced by steh₂tleh₂ ('heel'), not the goose word ǵʰh₂éns.
Adjectives agree with their nouns and the verb forms match the English.
'Where is the ford?' needs 3SG 'is', but h₁swós is 1DU 'we two are'.
Negation, subjunctives, and the possessive dual match the English.
'Shall I drive the cattle out?' needs the object 'cattle' (péḱu), but pnéwmn̥ means 'breath'.
'I shall pour it' needs 'pour' (ǵʰewdʰ-, as in ǵʰuddʰí); h₂téwǵoh₂ means 'spread terror'.
Dative, accusative, optative and subjunctive forms all match the English.
'I am not sad' is negated, but the PIE clause has no ne.
'In battle' needs locative singular (kh₃téwi, as used later), but kh₃túbʰos is dative/ablative plural.
'In a stone' is singular, but h₂éḱmonh₁e is a dual form.
'Do women climb onto roofs?' needs 'women' (gʷénh₂es), but méh₂teres means 'mothers'.
Locatives, instrumentals, and person-number forms match the English.
'A ram does not [grow]' is negated, but the second bʰuHyéti has no ne.
'Why does Sky not kill the wolves?' is negated, but the PIE clause has no ne.
'Do not lie down' is a prohibition with no mē, and the predicate 'hard' (dʰr̥ǵʰtéh₂) is feminine for a male husband.
'What will you pay?' is addressed to one kinsman, but kʷinéwete is 2PL.
Cases, datives, and subjunctive/imperative forms all match the English.
